title: Vishwakarma Jayanti 2026
author: Editorial Desk
summary: On 17 September BMS observes National Labour Day on Vishwakarma Jayanti: what the day means, why BMS chose it, and practical ideas for workplaces.
body:
Every year on **17 September**, workshops, factories and offices across the country pause for a day that mixes worship, celebration and reflection. It is **Vishwakarma Jayanti**, the day honouring the divine craftsman and architect, and it is the day that Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) observes as its **National Labour Day**. This post explains what the day is, why BMS chose it instead of 1 May, and how a union or an employer can make it more than a holiday.

## What Vishwakarma Jayanti is

Vishwakarma, or Vishvakarma, is the deity associated with craftsmanship, tools and building. The festival is called Vishvakarma Puja in many places, and it is usually held between 16 and 18 September, falling on Kanya Sankranti, the last day of the Hindu month of Bhadra. It is observed mostly by artisans, mechanics, smiths, welders, industrial and factory workers, engineers and architects. On the shop floor, people clean and decorate the workplace, set up a small shrine, and worship their tools and machines, praying for safe working conditions and for machines that run smoothly. Prasad is often shared among workers afterwards. In many parts of India, 17 September is a restricted holiday rather than a general one, and the festival is also observed in Nepal, where it is a full Government holiday ([Wikipedia: Vishvakarma Puja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vishvakarma_Puja)).

The word itself carries a thought. *Vishwa* means world and *karma* means work or action. A BMS leader's article on the subject describes Vishwakarma as the first labourer and a model for workers of every trade, and notes that some regions mark the day on other dates in the Hindu calendar, with 17 September adopted for uniformity ([Organiser, 17 September 2023](https://organiser.org/2023/09/17/119567/bharat/vishwakarma-jayanti-symbol-of-dignity/)).

## Why BMS observes it as National Labour Day

BMS's own pamphlet states that the organisation observes 17 September, Vishwakarma Jayanti, as National Labour Day ([VVGNLI: BMS at a Glance](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Bharatiya%20Mazdoor%20Sangh%20At%20a%20Glance.pdf)). The reasoning is laid out in articles by BMS leaders. The 1886 Chicago eight-hour-day agitation, which is the origin of 1 May, is described by one former BMS national president as a history that became entangled with party politics, and he says that BMS therefore does not observe May Day and treats Vishwakarma Jayanti as its labour day instead. He also says that several Indian States have declared it a Labour Day ([Organiser, 1 May 2023](https://organiser.org/2023/05/01/24511/bharat/why-doesnt-bms-celebrate-may-day-as-labour-day-explains-the-former-national-president-of-indias-biggest-labour-union/)). These are the arguments of BMS and its supporters, and others take a different view, but they explain the choice.

A second strand of the reasoning concerns outlook. BMS describes the workplace as an "industrial family" rather than a place of permanent conflict between owner and worker, and it speaks of work as a kind of service. In that view a festival that honours the skill of the hand and the tool fits better than a day framed around struggle. A 2026 opinion piece in the same magazine, written from a similar perspective, says that BMS and its founder Dattopant Thengadi chose Vishwakarma Jayanti as a national labour day for this reason ([Organiser, 17 September 2026](https://organiser.org/2026/09/17/380988/bharat/vishwakarma-puja-dattopant-thengadiji-vs-commies-communist-devaluation-of-dignity-and-selfhood/amp/)). That article is an opinion piece with strong views on other political groups, and we cite it only for what it says about BMS's own choice of the day.

The symbolism is also visible in the BMS logo. The pamphlet describes a raised fist between a wheel and a sheaf of grain, representing a balance between industrial development and agricultural prosperity, and a BMS history describes the fist and its opposable thumb as the origin of tools and machinery ([The Onward March of BMS](https://cdn.dbthengadi.in/scan/The_Onward_March_OF_BMS.pdf)).

## How the day is marked

A BMS report on a National Labour Day programme in Delhi, held on the eve of Vishwakarma Jayanti, shows the usual pattern. The BMS National President was chief guest, the Delhi State unit president presided, a zonal organising secretary was the main speaker, and former national office-bearers and leaders of federations attended ([BMS report](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=3683)). In districts and units, the programme is similar but smaller: a flag hoisting, a tool puja, speeches on the dignity of labour, and a community meal.

The occasion also coincides with Government attention to artisans. The PM Vishwakarma scheme was launched on 17 September 2023. It covers eighteen traditional trades, including blacksmiths, goldsmiths, potters, carpenters and sculptors, and offers registration with a certificate and ID card, skill training, a toolkit incentive of Rs 15,000, and collateral-free credit of up to Rs 1 lakh and then Rs 2 lakh at 5 per cent interest. It has an outlay of Rs 13,000 crore for the five years from 2023-24 to 2027-28 ([PIB document on the scheme](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2023/sep/doc2023918253401.pdf)). Unions that have artisans, tailors, carpenters or small-trade workers among their members can use the day to tell them about it.

## Practical ideas for unions

The day works best when it produces something useful that lasts beyond the evening. A few ideas:

- **Honour people.** Felicitate long-serving workers and apprentices, and give a place on the stage to the women and young workers who are rarely seen there.
- **Do a safety walk.** Before the puja, check machines, guards, wiring, fire extinguishers and first-aid boxes. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, which the Government brought into force on 21 November 2025, provides for safety committees in establishments with 500 or more workers and for free annual health check-ups for workers, according to the Labour Ministry's summary ([Labour Ministry release](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/pib2192463.pdf)). A union can use the day to ask whether those are in place.
- **Collect suggestions.** Keep a box or a register for workers' ideas on improving the workplace, with a promise to discuss them at the next meeting.
- **Organise a health camp or blood donation drive**, in partnership with a nearby hospital.
- **Run a short training session.** A one-hour talk on wage slips, provident fund passbooks or the appointment letter now required under the Codes is more useful than another speech.
- **Record the day.** Take a few photographs, note the number of workers present, and send a short report to the State unit.

## A note for employers

Give workers time to take part, and take part yourself. A workplace that celebrates its work is one that is more likely to do it well. The occasion costs little, yet it can improve the relationship between management and workers in a way that a notice board cannot. If you are an employer who also worships tools on this day, the strongest tribute you can offer is to make sure those tools and machines are safe for the people who use them.

## A thought for the year ahead

The day invites a simple question: what would it mean to treat work as the foundation of the world, as the name Vishwakarma suggests? For a union, it means respecting skill, paying a fair wage, and keeping the workplace safe. For a Government, it means designing schemes that reach the artisan in the village as well as the worker in the large factory. For all of us, it means remembering that behind every building, bridge, garment and machine there is a pair of hands, and that those hands deserve dignity.
